Jessica the jackrabbit wants to climb down a wall. The wall consists of 2026 horizontal layers stacked vertically. The $n$th layer from the top is partitioned into $2^n - 1$ identical rectangular bricks arranged side by side. Jessica begins in the topmost layer, which contains a single brick. A move consists of Jessica going down one layer to a brick that shares a side with the brick she is currently on.

Determine, with proof, the total number of distinct sequences of moves Jessica can take to reach the 2026th layer.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let the common width of the wall be \(1\).  
In layer \(n\), the number of bricks is

\[
M=2^n-1,
\]

so brick \(k\) in that layer has horizontal interval

\[
\left[\frac{k-1}{M},\frac{k}{M}\right], \qquad 1\le k\le M.
\]

Layer \(n+1\) has

\[
M'=2^{n+1}-1=2M+1
\]

bricks, and brick \(\ell\) in that layer has horizontal interval

\[
\left[\frac{\ell-1}{M'},\frac{\ell}{M'}\right].
\]

Two bricks in consecutive layers share a side exactly when their horizontal intervals overlap in a segment of positive length.

Now fix a brick \(k\) in layer \(n\). Measure horizontal position in units of the brick width in layer \(n+1\). Then the interval of brick \(k\) becomes

\[
\left[\frac{(k-1)M'}{M},\frac{kM'}{M}\right].
\]

Since \(M'=2M+1\), these endpoints are

\[
A=\frac{(k-1)(2M+1)}{M}=2k-2+\frac{k-1}{M},
\]
\[
B=\frac{k(2M+1)}{M}=2k+\frac{k}{M}.
\]

A brick \(\ell\) in layer \(n+1\) has interval \([\ell-1,\ell]\) in these units. It overlaps \([A,B]\) in a segment of positive length iff

\[
A<\ell \quad\text{and}\quad \ell-1<B,
\]

equivalently,

\[
A<\ell<B+1.
\]

Because \(1\le k\le M\),

\[
2k-2 \le A < 2k-1
\]

and

\[
2k+1 < B+1 \le 2k+2.
\]

Therefore the only integers \(\ell\) satisfying \(A<\ell<B+1\) are

\[
\ell=2k-1,\;2k,\;2k+1.
\]

These are all valid bricks in layer \(n+1\), and each indeed overlaps brick \(k\). Thus every brick has exactly \(3\) possible bricks in the next layer to move to.

Jessica starts in layer \(1\). To reach layer \(2026\), she must make exactly \(2025\) downward moves. At each move, no matter which brick she is on, there are exactly \(3\) choices for the next brick. Hence the number of possible sequences of moves is

\[
3^{2025}.
\]

\[
\boxed{3^{2025}}
\]
